title: Opinion: There will never be another Julian Alaphilippe
content:
Cyclist
Opinion: There will never be another Julian Alaphilippe

Here goes Robyn, romanticising another French cyclist. Well, Julian Alaphilippe was truly one-of-a-kind, and his immediate retirement marks the end of an era. It’s a damn shame.

Alaphilippe’s electrifying style of racing and ferociously attacking with his heart on his sleeve enchanted and captivated all who witnessed it. It was a match made in heaven that he spent the majority of his career with Soudal Quick-Step. A lack of general classification ambition allowed a young rider to flourish in an environment that promoted one-day explosivity delivered with a level of absurd panache that thrust him into the spotlight. Not that the opportunity for GC success never reared its head though.

In 2019, he dared to allow a nation to dream – one of maillot jaune hopes that had failed to materialise for France since 1985. Alaphilippe riding his way into the lead of the race come the finale of Stage 8 wasn’t surprising. Neither was his dogged determination to cling on as long as possible until he left claw marks in the yellow threads.

Somehow, in some way, he held off those breathing down his neck through the time-trial and into the Alps. Racing against the clock was not typically an Alaphilippe-favouring discipline. He made it so. After years plagued by a robotic Team Sky Grand Tour dominance, here was a man forcing his name to be shouted in a conversation that had nary allowed a whisper of it before.

It wasn’t to be. This doomed, aspirations-burning-bright-only-to-explode-into-embers archetype that had befallen his fellow countrymen – Thibaut Pinot being the Oscar winner of this unfortunate category – seemed destined to fall onto his shoulders at some point. It wasn’t straightforward either. A freak hailstorm caused a landslide on Stage 19 which cancelled the remaining 37.5km of the day and poured water on his GC fire, smoke plumes billowing into the air as Egan Bernal became the new maillot jaune thanks to his gap atop the Col de L’Iseran. So close yet so far. He didn’t leave with yellow, instead departing fifth overall with the overall combativity award in hand. Perhaps that sums it up the best.

It wasn’t all almosts, what-ifs and maybes. Alaphilippe shone throughout the Classics and amassed three victories at La Flèche Wallonne throughout his career, picking up his sole Monument of Milan-San Remo in a bunch sprint against the likes of Michał Kwiatkowski, Peter Sagan and Wout van Aert. Podium places do feature regularly in his palmarès in the Monuments too, showcasing just how close he repeatedly came, Liège-Bastogne-Liège and Il Lombardia also included.

Then there are the World Championships road titles in 2020 and 2021. It was a period in which Alaphilippe stood top of the pack, resplendent in the rainbow jersey which at times looked akin to a second skin.

But, like a fine wine, the bottle runs dry eventually. The wins died down after the Covid era came calling and he moved from WorldTour to ProTeam level with Tudor Pro Cycling in the twilight of his career. His last victory would be at the Grand Prix Cycliste de Québec in 2025 where, on a parcours with his name written all over it, he utilised the last ascent towards the line to jump clear in the final 1.5km.

At the crux of it all, Alaphilippe was a born entertainer. A showman that delivered some of cycling’s best moments throughout the 2010s, who on occasion had us wincing behind our fingers too at his audacity. I couldn’t get through this article without mentioning the premature celebration at Liège-Bastogne-Liège in 2020 that awarded the win to Primož Roglič instead and likely earned him an ear-clipping for his relegation at the Quick-Step bus.

Perhaps Alaphilippe deserved a better send-off – a definite retirement date that coincided with a guard of honour for all that he has given to the sport. The news appeared imminent after the recent Tour de France, when he admitted this was ‘certainly’ his last Tour after Stage 20 where he crossed the line beside fellow Frenchman Warren Barguil, arms around one another’s shoulders. However the images of him celebrating up Montmartre show that even though this would turn out to be the end despite a year remaining on his contract with Tudor Pro Cycling, he did at least end his career on his own terms, in his home country, surrounded by thousands of cheering fans. Not many can say that.

Plenty can try to emulate Alaphilippe, but there will only ever be one. And what a rider he was.
